subtopic_detail: Empirical antibiotics for meningitis in a young infant
stem:
A 6-week-old former term boy is brought to a regional ED with 12 hours of fever, poor feeding and increasing irritability. He is difficult to console, has a full anterior fontanelle and mottled peripheries. Capillary refill centrally is 3 seconds. Bloods and lumbar puncture have been obtained without difficulty and blood culture is drawn.

He is exclusively breastfed, has had all birth screening, and has no known immunodeficiency. His parents are Australian and there is no unusual travel or contact history.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 176/min, blood pressure 78/44 mmHg, respiratory rate 62/min, SpO2 97 percent on room air, temperature 38.8 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Alert but inconsolable; full anterior fontanelle; mottled peripheries; capillary refill 3 seconds centrally; no rash
data_table.Investigations: CSF: WCC 480/mm3 (85 percent neutrophils), protein 1.4 g/L (0.15-0.45), glucose 1.6 mmol/L with plasma 5.4 mmol/L; Gram stain negative; blood culture drawn; WCC 22 x10^9/L, CRP 88 mg/L (<5)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate empirical antibiotic regimen?

options.text: Intravenous ceftriaxone 100 mg/kg daily as sole empirical antimicrobial therapy
options.rationale: Ceftriaxone displaces bilirubin and is avoided in neonates and young infants where kernicterus risk remains; cefotaxime is preferred and Listeria cover is required. (Source: RCH CPG: Meningitis and encephalitis)

options.text: Intravenous benzylpenicillin 60 mg/kg every 6 hours and gentamicin 5 mg/kg daily
options.rationale: The neonatal sepsis penicillin-gentamicin combination is used up to 4 weeks; at 6 weeks the CSF-active third generation cephalosporin plus amoxicillin is preferred. (Source: RCH CPG: Meningitis and encephalitis)

options.text: Intravenous vancomycin 15 mg/kg every 6 hours as monotherapy for CSF cover
options.rationale: Vancomycin is added when pneumococcal disease is suspected and resistance is a concern; monotherapy misses Listeria and gram-negatives. (Source: RCH CPG: Meningitis and encephalitis)

options.text: Intravenous cefotaxime 50 mg/kg every 6 hours and amoxicillin 50 mg/kg every 6 hours
options.rationale: This combination is correct in principle but dexamethasone should be considered concurrently for infants with pneumococcal or Hib meningitis suspicion; the fully correct answer includes dexamethasone. (Source: RCH CPG: Meningitis and encephalitis)

options.text: Cefotaxime 50 mg/kg 6-hourly, amoxicillin 50 mg/kg 6-hourly plus dexamethasone
options.rationale: In infants under 3 months, empirical therapy is cefotaxime plus amoxicillin (Listeria cover); dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg 6-hourly for 4 days is given with or just before the first antibiotic if bacterial meningitis is suspected. (Source: RCH CPG: Meningitis and encephalitis)

explanation.summary: Empirical antibiotic therapy for suspected bacterial meningitis in an infant aged over 4 weeks and under 3 months is intravenous cefotaxime plus amoxicillin to cover common pathogens (Streptococcus pneumoniae, Neisseria meningitidis, group B streptococcus, Escherichia coli and Listeria monocytogenes). Ceftriaxone is avoided in neonates because of bilirubin displacement and kernicterus risk. Dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg every 6 hours for 4 days is recommended when Haemophilus influenzae type b or pneumococcal meningitis is suspected, ideally given with or just before the first antibiotic dose to reduce neurological sequelae.
key_points: Cefotaxime plus amoxicillin covers common pathogens under 3 months.
Ceftriaxone avoided in neonates because of bilirubin displacement.
Amoxicillin covers Listeria in under 3 months.
Dexamethasone with or before first antibiotic when bacterial meningitis suspected.
explanation.pearls: In a young infant with suspected meningitis, start cefotaxime plus amoxicillin plus dexamethasone concurrently; do not use ceftriaxone under 3 months and do not delay dexamethasone until organism is known.

stem:
A 4-year-old boy on maintenance chemotherapy for acute lymphoblastic leukaemia was in the same primary school classroom as another child who developed a chickenpox rash yesterday. His medical team confirms he received VZV vaccination pre-diagnosis but has not had chickenpox. He has been on maintenance chemotherapy for 8 months and his most recent lymphocyte count was 0.6 x10^9/L. Contact occurred 20 hours ago in an indoor setting for over an hour.

He is currently well with no fever, malaise or rash. His mother contacted the oncology fellow this morning to ask what to do.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 100/min, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 22/min, SpO2 100 percent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Well; no rash; oropharynx clear; abdomen soft; no lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: Absolute lymphocyte count 0.6 x10^9/L (2.0-8.0); recent varicella IgG antibody titre pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate post-exposure management?

options.text: Zoster immunoglobulin (ZIG) intramuscular within 96 hours of contact today
options.rationale: ZIG is indicated for significant exposure in a susceptible immunocompromised child and is most effective within 96 hours (up to 10 days); on maintenance chemotherapy, prior vaccination cannot be assumed to confer protection. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook: Varicella)

options.text: Give the varicella live-attenuated vaccine within 5 days of the contact today
options.rationale: Live vaccines are contraindicated during chemotherapy because of dissemination risk; ZIG is the passive prophylaxis choice. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook: Varicella)

options.text: Start oral aciclovir 20 mg/kg 4 times daily for 7 days immediately as prophylaxis
options.rationale: Aciclovir may be used from day 7 to 14 post-exposure as an alternative when ZIG is unavailable; ZIG is first-line if within window. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook: Varicella)

options.text: No action; the vaccine received before diagnosis provides adequate ongoing protection
options.rationale: Chemotherapy suppresses vaccine-induced immunity; a pre-diagnosis vaccine cannot be assumed protective and passive prophylaxis is required. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook: Varicella)

options.text: Admit today for intravenous immunoglobulin and prolonged inpatient monitoring
options.rationale: IVIG is not the equivalent product for VZV post-exposure prophylaxis; specific ZIG is used and can be given as an outpatient. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook: Varicella)

explanation.summary: Post-exposure varicella prophylaxis in an immunocompromised child uses zoster immunoglobulin (ZIG) intramuscularly, ideally within 96 hours of significant contact and up to 10 days. Significant contact is defined as face-to-face contact of 5 minutes or more, or over 1 hour in the same indoor space. Prior varicella vaccination cannot be assumed protective during chemotherapy because immunosuppression suppresses vaccine responses. Live vaccines are contraindicated during chemotherapy. Oral aciclovir from day 7 to 14 post-exposure is an alternative if ZIG is unavailable.
key_points: ZIG within 96 hours (up to 10 days) for immunocompromised contacts.
Significant contact: 5 min face-to-face or 1 hour indoors.
Live vaccines contraindicated during chemotherapy.
Aciclovir day 7 to 14 is second-line if ZIG unavailable.
explanation.pearls: For an immunocompromised child exposed to varicella, arrange ZIG within 96 hours; do not rely on pre-chemotherapy vaccine history and do not use live vaccine.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Chickenpox exposure in an immunocompromised child

subtopic_detail: Tubal ectopic pregnancy medical vs surgical decision
stem:
A 28-year-old G2P1 presents to the early pregnancy assessment service 6 weeks and 4 days by LMP with vaginal spotting for 3 days. She has no acute pain and is haemodynamically stable. A transvaginal ultrasound shows an empty uterus, a 22 mm right adnexal mass with no yolk sac and no cardiac activity, and 15 mL of free fluid in the pouch of Douglas. Her serum beta-hCG today is 2400 IU/L, up from 2100 IU/L 48 hours ago.

Her first pregnancy 3 years ago was a normal vaginal delivery. She has no significant medical history and is not on medication. She has stable social supports and can attend for follow-up.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 76/min, blood pressure 118/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Alert, well; abdomen soft with mild right iliac fossa tenderness; no rebound or guarding; speculum shows minimal old blood in vault
data_table.Investigations: Beta-hCG 2400 IU/L (was 2100 IU/L 48h ago); Hb 128 g/L (115-165), platelets 244 x10^9/L, LFTs and creatinine within normal limits; blood group A positive; TVUS confirms right tubal ectopic 22 mm without cardiac activity

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Single dose intramuscular methotrexate 50 mg/m2 with day 4 and 7 hCG follow-up
options.rationale: RANZCOG criteria for methotrexate: beta-hCG under 5000 IU/L, mass under 3.5 cm, no foetal cardiac activity, no significant pain, stable, reliable follow-up, no methotrexate contraindications; this patient meets all criteria. (Source: RANZCOG Ectopic Pregnancy Guideline)

options.text: Expectant management with 48-hourly beta-hCG until decline is confirmed
options.rationale: Expectant management is limited to patients with clearly falling hCG or hCG under 1500 with no mass; this patient's hCG is rising and a mass is visible. (Source: RANZCOG Ectopic Pregnancy Guideline)

options.text: Laparoscopic salpingectomy of the right tube on the next elective operating list
options.rationale: Surgery is preferred when RANZCOG methotrexate criteria are not met (hCG 5000 IU/L or above, mass 3.5 cm or above, cardiac activity, pain, instability) or when medical management is contraindicated; this patient qualifies for medical. (Source: RANZCOG Ectopic Pregnancy Guideline)

options.text: Laparoscopic salpingostomy with intraoperative hCG tissue sampling for histology
options.rationale: Salpingostomy is a fertility-preserving surgical option; medical therapy is still preferred where criteria are met to avoid anaesthetic and surgical morbidity. (Source: RANZCOG Ectopic Pregnancy Guideline)

options.text: Give mifepristone and misoprostol regimen for medical termination of pregnancy
options.rationale: Mifepristone-misoprostol is used for intrauterine pregnancy termination, not tubal ectopic; it does not treat the ectopic. (Source: RANZCOG Ectopic Pregnancy Guideline)

explanation.summary: RANZCOG criteria for methotrexate treatment of tubal ectopic pregnancy require haemodynamic stability, no significant pain, beta-hCG under 5000 IU/L, tubal mass under 3.5 cm, no foetal cardiac activity, no free-fluid haemoperitoneum, reliable patient follow-up, and no methotrexate contraindications (normal LFTs, renal function, WCC, no active peptic ulcer). Single dose methotrexate 50 mg/m2 IM is the standard regimen with day 4 and 7 beta-hCG measurement, expecting a 15 percent fall between day 4 and day 7. A second dose is given if the fall is inadequate. Surgical management (salpingectomy preferred; salpingostomy for fertility preservation with contralateral disease) is indicated when medical criteria are not met.
key_points: Methotrexate criteria: hCG under 5000, mass under 3.5 cm, no cardiac activity, stable.
Day 4 and day 7 hCG check with expected 15 percent fall.
Salpingectomy preferred surgically; salpingostomy for fertility preservation.
Expectant only if hCG clearly falling or under 1500 without mass.
explanation.pearls: The RANZCOG bhCG threshold for surgical management of tubal ectopic is 5000 IU/L or above; below 5000 with normal LFTs, renal function, no cardiac activity and mass under 3.5 cm, single dose methotrexate is first-line.

stem:
A 34-year-old man with treatment-resistant schizophrenia has been stable on clozapine 400 mg at night for 18 months. He was admitted to a medical ward 3 days ago with community-acquired pneumonia and clozapine was withheld throughout that admission. He is now afebrile on oral antibiotics, medically stable, and has returned to the mental health unit today. He has had no seizures. His last blood monitoring 6 weeks ago showed a neutrophil count in the green range.

He is settled without acute psychotic symptoms, sleeps well and eats normal meals. He is smoking again on the unit balcony.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 82/min, blood pressure 118/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Alert, oriented; no chest signs on auscultation; no meningism
data_table.Investigations: FBC neutrophils 3.4 x10^9/L (2.0-7.5), platelets 210 x10^9/L; CRP 22 mg/L (<5); ECG QTc 420 ms; clozapine last dose 72 hours ago

lead_in: What is the most appropriate approach to restarting clozapine?

options.text: Restart clozapine at the previous maintenance dose of 400 mg orally at night tonight
options.rationale: Any interruption of clozapine of 48 hours or more requires retitration from a low starting dose (typically 12.5 to 25 mg); resuming full dose risks hypotension, cardiac collapse and myocarditis. (Source: Clozapine RCM protocol; RANZCP)

options.text: Restart clozapine at 12.5 mg orally at night and retitrate over 1 to 2 weeks
options.rationale: Any clozapine break of 48 hours or more mandates restart from 12.5 mg with slow retitration (usually 25 mg then 50 mg over subsequent days), monitoring BP and pulse; abrupt full-dose resumption is contraindicated. (Source: Clozapine RCM protocol; RANZCP)

options.text: Restart clozapine at 200 mg orally as a single dose tonight then reassess tomorrow
options.rationale: 200 mg exceeds the safe restart threshold after a 48-hour or longer break; hypotension and QTc effects are unpredictable at this dose after washout. (Source: Clozapine RCM protocol; RANZCP)

options.text: Switch to oral olanzapine 20 mg nightly and cease clozapine permanently now
options.rationale: Clozapine is definitive treatment for treatment-resistant schizophrenia; permanent cessation for a temporary medical interruption is not indicated. (Source: Clozapine RCM protocol; RANZCP)

options.text: Delay restart until FBC monitoring is repeated and the C-reactive protein normalises
options.rationale: Neutrophils are in the green range and CRP does not preclude restart; delay increases relapse risk when retitration can safely begin. (Source: Clozapine RCM protocol; RANZCP)

explanation.summary: Clozapine has a narrow therapeutic index and rapid loss of tolerance to hypotensive, cardiac and sedative effects. Any interruption of 48 hours or more requires restart at 12.5 mg with slow retitration over 1 to 2 weeks. Smoking induces CYP1A2 and lowers clozapine levels; smoking cessation during admission raises levels and dose reduction is often needed on quitting. Weekly full blood count monitoring restarts at the beginning of retitration (or aligns with local Clozapine Patient Monitoring Service requirements). Cardiac monitoring including ECG for QTc and troponin for myocarditis surveillance is undertaken over the first weeks.
key_points: Interruption 48 hours or more requires restart at 12.5 mg.
Retitration typically 12.5, 25, 50 mg over days.
Smoking induces CYP1A2; ceasing to smoke raises clozapine levels.
Weekly FBC monitoring restarts with retitration.
explanation.pearls: After any clozapine break of 48 hours or more, restart at 12.5 mg regardless of previous stable dose; a full-dose restart risks hypotension, sedation and myocarditis.

stem:
A 62-year-old woman on lithium carbonate 750 mg nightly for bipolar I disorder for 12 years presents with 3 days of coarse tremor, worsening confusion, unsteady gait and vomiting. She started a thiazide diuretic 2 weeks ago for hypertension. Her last outpatient lithium level 6 weeks ago was 0.7 mmol/L. On examination she is drowsy, moves all four limbs but is ataxic, and has hyperreflexia and myoclonic jerks.

She has no fever and no rash. She lives alone and has been unable to keep down water. Her partner brought her to hospital when she became confused overnight.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 108/min, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 22/min, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temperature 37.2 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Drowsy but rousable, GCS 13; coarse tremor and myoclonus; ataxic gait; brisk reflexes without clonus; dry mucous membranes
data_table.Investigations: Serum lithium 3.6 mmol/L (0.4-1.0); creatinine 168 micromol/L (60-110) up from 82 baseline; sodium 148 mmol/L (135-145); ECG QTc 470 ms; no ischaemic changes

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Cease lithium and give intravenous 0.9 percent sodium chloride at 200 mL/hour alone
options.rationale: IV fluids and lithium cessation are essential but insufficient alone at this level and with neurotoxicity and renal impairment; haemodialysis is required. (Source: Australian eTG: Toxicology - Lithium)

options.text: Give activated charcoal 50 g orally and observe with 4-hourly lithium concentrations
options.rationale: Charcoal does not bind lithium; it has no role in decontamination for chronic lithium toxicity. (Source: Australian eTG: Toxicology - Lithium)

options.text: Arrange urgent haemodialysis and cease lithium with concurrent intravenous fluids
options.rationale: Haemodialysis is indicated for lithium level over 2.5 mmol/L with symptoms, level over 4 mmol/L regardless, or level over 2.5 mmol/L with renal impairment; this patient meets criteria. (Source: Australian eTG: Toxicology - Lithium; EXTRIP guidelines)

options.text: Continue lithium at half the previous dose after starting intravenous rehydration
options.rationale: Continuing lithium at any dose during acute toxicity is unsafe; the drug must be withheld. (Source: Australian eTG: Toxicology - Lithium)

options.text: Give whole bowel irrigation with polyethylene glycol until effluent runs clear now
options.rationale: Whole bowel irrigation is considered for acute massive ingestion of sustained-release preparations; not helpful in chronic toxicity from routine dosing. (Source: Australian eTG: Toxicology - Lithium)

explanation.summary: Chronic lithium toxicity is common in patients on long-term therapy after a new nephrotoxic or diuretic medication, dehydration, or intercurrent illness. Haemodialysis is indicated for lithium concentration over 4 mmol/L regardless of symptoms, or over 2.5 mmol/L with severe neurological features, renal impairment or haemodynamic instability, or when levels are expected to remain elevated for a prolonged period. Charcoal does not bind lithium. Whole bowel irrigation may be considered for acute massive sustained-release ingestion. Rebound rises in lithium after dialysis are common; extended sessions or repeat dialysis are often required.
key_points: Dialysis indicated: level over 4 always; over 2.5 with symptoms or AKI.
Chronic toxicity often precipitated by dehydration, NSAID, ACEi, thiazide.
Charcoal does not bind lithium.
Rebound rise post-dialysis is common; extended or repeat sessions needed.
explanation.pearls: For a chronic lithium toxicity patient on a thiazide with level over 2.5 mmol/L, neurotoxicity and rising creatinine, arrange urgent haemodialysis; do not just fluid-resuscitate.

subtopic_detail: Valproate in a woman planning pregnancy
stem:
A 29-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder has been stable on sodium valproate 1000 mg daily for 4 years without relapse. She reports today that she and her partner are planning to start trying for a pregnancy in the next 3 months. She has a body mass index of 26, no other medical problems and does not smoke. Her last mood episode was a manic episode requiring inpatient admission 4 years ago.

She is euthymic today with no psychotic features. Her current supports are strong and she is engaged with a private psychiatrist and general practitioner.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 76/min, blood pressure 118/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Alert, euthymic; mental state examination unremarkable; no acute risk features
data_table.Investigations: TSH within normal limits; beta-hCG negative today; LFTs within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate mood-stabiliser change?

options.text: Continue valproate at current dose and arrange preconception folate supplementation
options.rationale: Valproate is highly teratogenic (neural tube defects, cardiac and skeletal defects, neurodevelopmental effects); it is contraindicated in women planning pregnancy where alternatives exist. (Source: RANZCP Perinatal Psychiatry Guidelines)

options.text: Reduce valproate to 500 mg daily and add high-dose folate 5 mg daily orally
options.rationale: Dose reduction does not eliminate teratogenicity; high-dose folate does not neutralise valproate neural tube defect risk. (Source: RANZCP Perinatal Psychiatry Guidelines)

options.text: Cross-taper to lithium carbonate with monitoring of levels, thyroid and renal function
options.rationale: Lithium is the safest mood stabiliser in pregnancy planning after valproate cessation, with the smallest absolute teratogenicity signal (Ebstein anomaly around 1 in 1000 to 2000) and strong evidence for bipolar prevention. (Source: RANZCP Perinatal Psychiatry Guidelines)

options.text: Cross-taper to carbamazepine 200 mg twice daily with slow monthly dose titration
options.rationale: Carbamazepine is also teratogenic (neural tube defects, craniofacial malformations, developmental delay); it does not solve the problem. (Source: RANZCP Perinatal Psychiatry Guidelines)

options.text: Cease valproate now with no replacement and monitor for relapse with therapy alone
options.rationale: Ceasing mood stabiliser without replacement in bipolar I with prior severe manic episode carries very high relapse risk; a replacement is essential. (Source: RANZCP Perinatal Psychiatry Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Sodium valproate is contraindicated in women of childbearing potential planning pregnancy because of teratogenicity (roughly 10 percent risk of major congenital malformations including neural tube defects, and a well-documented neurodevelopmental effect). Australian guidelines require pregnancy prevention programmes if valproate is unavoidable. For a woman with bipolar I disorder planning pregnancy, lithium is generally the safest evidence-based mood stabiliser: teratogenicity risk (Ebstein anomaly) is smaller than previously estimated at around 1 in 1000 to 2000, and its efficacy for relapse prevention is strong. Cross-tapering is done gradually to maintain stability, with regular level monitoring in pregnancy and postpartum dose adjustment.
key_points: Valproate is contraindicated in women planning pregnancy where alternatives exist.
Carbamazepine is also teratogenic; it is not an acceptable substitute.
Lithium is the safest bipolar mood stabiliser in pregnancy planning.
Ebstein anomaly with lithium is around 1 in 1000 to 2000, not 1 in 100.
explanation.pearls: In a woman with bipolar I disorder planning pregnancy on valproate, cross-taper to lithium; do not switch to carbamazepine and do not just reduce the valproate dose.

sources.label: Australian eTG: Psychotropic - Bipolar disorder in pregnancy
